title: "Geese: a fixed effect and concentration dependence"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Geese: a fixed effect and concentration dependence}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(MixSIARPFN)
ok <- MixSIARPFN:::networks_ready()   # the code needs the networks (see pfn_networks())
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = ok,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "100%")
num <- function(x, digits = 2) if (ok) format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits) else "?"
```

This follows MixSIAR's geese example (Inger et al. 2006 data, as analysed in Stock et
al. 2018): 251 geese in 8 groups, two tracers (δ¹³C and δ¹⁵N) and four food sources
(grass and three algae: Enteromorpha, *Ulva lactuca* and *Zostera*). Group is a fixed
effect, the sources' elemental concentrations differ (concentration dependence), and
the error structure is Residual only. Only the fitting call differs from MixSIAR's
vignette: `run_pfn()` in place of `write_JAGS_model()` and `run_model()`.

## The data

```{r load, eval = TRUE}
mix <- load_mix_data(
  filename = system.file("extdata", "geese_consumer.csv", package = "MixSIARPFN"),
  iso_names = c("d13C", "d15N"), factors = "Group", fac_random = FALSE,
  fac_nested = FALSE, cont_effects = NULL)
source <- load_source_data(
  filename = system.file("extdata", "geese_sources.csv", package = "MixSIARPFN"),
  source_factors = NULL, conc_dep = TRUE, data_type = "means", mix)
discr <- load_discr_data(
  filename = system.file("extdata", "geese_discrimination.csv", package = "MixSIARPFN"),
  mix)
mix
source
```

The isospace plot shows the geese, coloured by group, and the source means after
discrimination, with ±1 SD. With four sources and two tracers the data cannot pin
down every proportion (that needs at most one more source than tracers), so some of
the diet is set by the prior and the sources' spread:

```{r isospace, eval = TRUE, fig.height = 5}
plot_data(mix = mix, source = source, discr = discr)
```

## Fitting the model

As in MixSIAR's vignette, Residual only error (`process_err = FALSE`) and the
uninformative prior:

```{r fit}
time <- system.time(
  fit <- run_pfn(mix, source, discr, alpha.prior = 1,
                 resid_err = TRUE, process_err = FALSE)
)
fit
```

The fit took `r num(time[["elapsed"]], 1)` seconds.

## Results

```{r output, results = "hide", fig.show = "hide"}
out <- output_pfn(fit, mix, source,
                  output_options = list(summary_save = FALSE, plot_post_save_pdf = FALSE))
```

```{r summary-table}
knitr::kable(round(summary_table(fit), 3))
```

With a fixed effect, MixSIAR's global diet is the diet of the first group, so the
plots below show the eight groups:

```{r group-plot, fig.height = 6}
out$plots$Group
```

Each is a **marginal** posterior: the network does not give joint draws, so the
marginal means of one group's diet need not sum to exactly 1, and sums or ratios of
proportions cannot be computed from the output.

## Comparison with MixSIAR

```{r reference}
ref <- mixsiar_reference("geese")
cmp <- compare_mixsiar(fit, ref$draws, ref$summary)
```

MixSIAR `r if (ok) ref$info$mixsiar` fitted the same model with
`r if (ok) ref$info$chains` chains of `r if (ok) format(ref$info$chain_length, big.mark = ",")`
iterations (burn-in `r if (ok) format(ref$info$burn, big.mark = ",")`), which took about
`r num(ref$info$minutes / 60, 1)` hours (largest Gelman-Rubin diagnostic
`r num(ref$info$max_psrf, 3)`). MixSIARPFN took `r num(time[["elapsed"]], 1)` seconds.

Means, SDs, 95% intervals and the Wasserstein-1 distance (W1: how far, on average,
one posterior's mass has to move to match the other, on the proportion scale):

```{r compare-table}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  quantity = cmp$name,
  `MixSIARPFN mean` = round(cmp$pfn_mean, 3), `MixSIAR mean` = round(cmp$mixsiar_mean, 3),
  `MixSIARPFN SD` = round(cmp$pfn_sd, 3), `MixSIAR SD` = round(cmp$mixsiar_sd, 3),
  `MixSIARPFN 95% CI` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", cmp$pfn_q2.5, cmp$pfn_q97.5),
  `MixSIAR 95% CI` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", cmp$mixsiar_q2.5, cmp$mixsiar_q97.5),
  W1 = round(cmp$w1, 3), check.names = FALSE))
```

```{r compare-group, fig.height = 8}
plot_compare(fit, ref$draws, block = "Group")
```

```{r compare-means, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_compare(fit, ref$draws, type = "means")
```

```{r numbers, include = FALSE}
by_source <- split(cmp, cmp$source)
gap <- function(d) mean(abs(d$pfn_mean - d$mixsiar_mean))
algae <- cmp[cmp$source != "Grass", ]
worst <- cmp[which.max(abs(cmp$pfn_mean - cmp$mixsiar_mean)), ]
```

**What this shows.** Grass, the source the data pin down best, is close in every
group: MixSIARPFN's means differ from MixSIAR's by `r num(gap(by_source$Grass))` on
average, though its posteriors are wider (median SD ratio
`r num(median(by_source$Grass$sd_ratio))`). The three algae trade off against each
other, since four sources cannot all be determined from two tracers, and there the
two fits differ more: mean difference
`r num(gap(algae))`, median SD ratio `r num(median(algae$sd_ratio))`, and the largest
difference is `r if (ok) sub("^p\\.", "", worst$name)` (`r num(worst$pfn_mean)`
against `r num(worst$mixsiar_mean)`). For data like these, where sources overlap, MixSIARPFN gives a quick
first answer and a MixSIAR run the more precise one.
